extracted.intended_audience: architects, architecture students, critics, and informed readers of architectural criticism
extracted.subtask_description: Close critical analysis of St. Mark's and the Venetian 'incrusted' school: judge buildings first as constructed/decorative works of art, then as expressive/functional places of worship; derive practical rules for designing and assessing incrusted architecture (use of marble facing, string courses, conservation of fragments, color use).

rubrics_metrics.name: Two-stage evaluation: form then expression
rubrics_metrics.description: In every building we should first form a judgment of its construction and decorative merit considered merely as a work of art; and then examine in what degree it fulfills its expressional purposes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge the building 'merely as a piece of architecture' first, and only afterwards estimate its fitness for its special duty (e.g., as a place of worship) and its relation to other cathedral-types. This separation prevents conflating abstract architectural perfection with current use or devotional effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judge architecture on abstract grounds, not present usefulness
rubrics_metrics.description: The merits and meaning of the architecture must be pursued without reference to its present usefulness; we must conduct the inquiry on abstract grounds to determine whether neglect signifies decline or whether the building is a relic of another age.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not let contemporary neglect, changed liturgical practice, or current levels of popular understanding determine the architectural judgment. Analyze construction, form, and principles independently of present congregational behaviour or civic condition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identification of incrustation as the primary characteristic
rubrics_metrics.description: The first broad characteristic and root of many peculiarities of St. Mark's is its confessed incrustation: the ruling principle is the incrustation of brick with more precious materials.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish clearly between the 'incrusted' and the 'massive' families of buildings: in incrusted buildings the substance is of two kinds (internal and external) and decoration is founded on this duplicity. Fix the legitimate characteristics of each family before critique; intermediate examples exist but should not obscure the distinction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Understand and accept the duplicity (brick body + marble armor)
rubrics_metrics.description: Incrusted architecture assumes that the body and availing strength of the edifice are to be in brick, and that this under muscular power of brickwork is to be clothed with the defence and the brightness of the marble.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Accept this condition when judging or designing: consider thin facing as 'armor' or 'skin' rather than structural mass. Once accepted, the consequent fitnesses and laws of the structure (proportions, delicate binding elements, methods of attachment) follow naturally.

rubrics_metrics.name: Law I — light, delicate plinths and cornices for binding the armor
rubrics_metrics.description: The plinths and cornices used for binding the armor are to be light and delicate. A certain thickness, at least two or three inches, must be required in the covering pieces to prevent fracture and allow for wear of time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Binding pieces must not be trusted to cement alone: they should be connected to the mass they protect by binding cornices and string courses and by mutual support aided (but not solely dependent on) rivetings. These string courses and binding plinths should be of such proportions that they are visibly incapable of taking important structural work—so as to preserve the 'honesty' of the incrusted style.

rubrics_metrics.name: Structural honesty in incrustation (no pretence of solidity)
rubrics_metrics.description: The incrusted style should not be insincere; the external slabs and armor should show honest attachment and accommodation to the internal substance rather than pretending to be solid throughout.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Fasten slabs openly (e.g., 'fastened to the next by a confessed rivet') and accommodate joints visibly to internal contours. The observer should not be deceived into mistaking the facing for structural mass—treat armor as armor (honesty of construction).

rubrics_metrics.name: Conservation and reuse of sculptured fragments
rubrics_metrics.description: Where architects inherit sculptured fragments from older buildings, they should preserve and reuse them rather than sawing them up to avoid interference with new designs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer inserting fragmentary sculptures and adapting new forms to available pieces, so as to 'save every relic with which he was entrusted.' Anti-pattern: an architect who cuts old marbles into new fragments to gratify personal design ambition (destroying noble work). This practice contributed to Venetian splendor and associative value.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of materials as chromatic decoration ('cakes of very hard color')
rubrics_metrics.description: Treat jasper, alabaster, porphyry, etc., as 'cakes of very hard color'—portions of precious stone are to be ground down or cut off to 'paint' the walls; the incrusted school is the only one in which perfect and permanent chromatic decoration is possible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognition of color importance is essential. Those lacking the perception of color are incapable of judging buildings like St. Mark's. Design and critique should account for the chromatic system: marbles and colored stones are not merely status materials but deliberate elements of permanent coloration and composition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Separate assessment of fitness for worship/expression
rubrics_metrics.description: After judging architectural construction and decorative merit, separately estimate the building's fitness for its special duty as a place of worship and its influence on popular devotional feeling.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Observe that architectural impressiveness and pictorial Scripture histories do not necessarily translate into understood or effective devotional influence for the contemporary populace. Consider psychological and popular effects (darkness, torchlight, precious materials, incense, music) as 'stage properties' of superstition—distinct from formal architectural merits.
